title: Terminal cuts, direct bounds and a witness in the stack row space

add.label: Lemma B.2
add.name: Generic bound
add.proof:
The formula for $\varepsilon_f$ is positive since $D<q$.
The polynomial given by the formula for $E$ has quadratic coefficient $(\theta+10\varepsilon_f)/2$.
This coefficient is positive since $\theta>0$. Thus $E$ is convex.
By (P5), $E(2)\le 2^{-\lambda}$.
Adding the two inequalities of (P5) gives $E(2^{\lambda+1})\le 1$.
The affine function $u/2^{\lambda+1}$ takes those upper bounds at the two endpoints.
Convexity bounds $E$ by this affine function on $[2,2^{\lambda+1}]$.
Taking $u=2Q+2$ gives the claim.
add.explain: Proves the bound used on the outgoing edge.

add.name: Heavy stacks
add.label: Lemma B.8
add.statement:
Let the parameters satisfy (P3), and let $\mathbf{W}$ be a heavy stack.

 
(a) $\operatorname{rank} \mathbf{W} \le 3$.
(b) Every kernel vector $v$ in the row space of $\mathbf{W}$ has a short multiple.
(c) If $x$ is a short multiple of a kernel vector, then $\hat x \in R^\ell$, with the $\hat x_j$ of Definition 5.1 over $\mathbb{Z}$, solves MSIS for the matrix $A$ of the columns $1, \dots, \ell$ of $M$ (Definition 3.3): $0 < \|\hat x\|_\infty \le \beta$ and $A \hat x = 0 \bmod q$.
add.explain: Directly counts stack fibers and applies the inverse theorem to the kernel vector.
add.proof:
Suppose the matrix formed by stacking the rows of the $W_c$ has rank at least four.
Choose four independent columns including column $0$ if it is nonzero.
Fix the independent draws corresponding to the other columns, with $r_\star$ corresponding to column $0$ in $\mathcal D_g$.
If column $0$ is unchosen, it is zero.
A fiber prescribes at most one residue tuple in the four chosen columns by their independence.
The residues at the chosen nonzero indices determine at most one draw each since $g<q$.
If column $0$ was chosen, its residue determines at most one independent draw, since in $\mathcal D_g$ the remaining entries now fix the shift from $r_\star$.
Each fiber therefore contains at most a fraction $g^{-4}$ of the draws.
Condition (I5) gives $g^{-4}<\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
The definition $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}=\theta-100\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ gives $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}<\theta$ since $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}>0$.
This fiber bound contradicts heaviness.

Let $v$ be a kernel vector in the row space.
The constant coefficient of $z(v)=0$ gives $v_0=0$.
As $v$ lies in the row space, $v^\top r$ is constant on each stack fiber.
The heaviest fiber then gives $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top)\ge\operatorname{gp}(\mathbf W)$.
Heaviness gives $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top)>\theta$.
The incoming inverse bound supplies a short multiple.

For any short multiple $x$, its reduction lies in the kernel of $z$ by linearity.
The constant coefficient then gives $x_0=0\bmod q$.
The bound $|x_0|\le\beta<q$ implies $x_0=0$ over the integers.
The remaining coefficients of $z(x\bmod q)$ are those of $A\hat x$ by the definition of the forms at $x_0=0$.
Thus $A\hat x=0\bmod q$.
The short multiple has nonzero reduction, so $x\ne 0$. 
Packing $x_1,\dots,x_N$ with zero padding preserves $0<\|x\|_\infty\le\beta$.

add.label: Lemma 4.7
add.name: QAP criterion by coset averaging
add.explain: Uses simultaneous divisibility and the root bound on the coset average.
add.statement:
For admissible evaluation points and symmetric $W$, passing is equivalent to divisibility of $P_W-Z_0R$ by $Z$ for an allowed $R$.
Passing is also equivalent to divisibility of $P_W-\chi L_\rho-Z_0R$ by $Z(X)(X-\rho)$ for an allowed $R$ and a scalar $\chi$.
The respective quotients have degrees below $D$ and $D-1$.
Both divisions require $R=R_W$, and the second requires $\chi=W_{00}$. For a witness $w$, both divisions exist for $W=ww^\top$ with $\chi=1$.
add.proof:
By the QAP table, $P_W-Z_0R$ vanishes on $\mathcal P_0\setminus\{\rho\}$ exactly when the Booleanity tests hold.
On the cosets, vanishing requires exactly the interpolant $R_W$ because $R$ has degree below $\nu n_{\mathsf c}$.
The factor theorem therefore gives divisibility by $Z$ exactly when the Booleanity tests hold and $R=R_W$.
By the QAP table, passing the constraints means that the coset sums of $R_W$ vanish.
The polynomial $\sum_{\xi\in\mathcal G}R_W(\xi X)$ takes those sums at all $\nu n_{\mathsf c}$ coset points.
It vanishes at those points exactly when it is zero by its degree bound.
The monomial sum rule shows that it is zero exactly when $R_W$ has no exponent divisible by $\nu$, since $\nu\ne0$ in $\mathbb F_q$.
Thus the interpolant is allowed exactly when the constraint tests hold.
Interpolation gives $L_\rho=Z/Z(\rho)$.
Subtracting $\chi L_\rho$ therefore preserves divisibility by $Z$ in both directions.
The QAP table gives $P_W(\rho)-\chi L_\rho(\rho)-Z_0(\rho)R(\rho)=W_{00}-\chi$.
Given divisibility by $Z$, the factor theorem makes the extra factor $X-\rho$ equivalent to $\chi=W_{00}$.
The degrees of the numerators are at most $2D-2$ by the defining degrees.
Subtracting the respective divisor degrees gives the two bounds.
A witness $w$ has $w_0=1$, which gives $(ww^\top)_{00}=1$.
On its moment matrix, the Booleanity tests give $w_j^2-w_j=0$.
Each constraint test gives $\sum_f a_{t,f}(w)b_{t,f}(w)-w_0c_t(w)=0$ by the witness property.
Thus both divisions exist by the equivalences.

add.label: Lemma B.6
add.name: A witness in the row space
add.explain: Uses the symmetric trilinear form forced by the ties and the Boolean coordinates.
add.statement: A nonzero usable stack of rank at most three with no kernel vector in its row space has a witness of $S$ in that row space.
add.proof:
Let $\mathcal V$ be the row space of the stack and $d$ its dimension.
Take a basis matrix $\mathcal U$ for $\mathcal V$ with rows $u_i$.
Take $W_s$ to be $W_U,W_V,\sigma^{n/2+1}(W_U)$ in the respective order $s\in I=\{n/2-1,n/2,n/2+1\}$.
Put $z_s=\sigma^s(z)$ and $h_s=\mathcal U^\top z_s$.
The three substitutions $-T/\omega,-T,-\omega T$ act as the corresponding powers of $\sigma$ modulo $P$, since $\omega^{n/2}=-1$ and $\sigma(T)=\omega T$.
Thus the vanishing of the three tie polynomials modulo $P$ yields $W_s z_{s'}=W_{s'}z_s$ for each pair in $I$.
The entries of $h_0$ are independent over $\mathbb F_q$ because a nonzero combination of the basis vectors cannot lie in the kernel of $z$.
Since $\mathcal U$ is over $\mathbb F_q$, $h_s=\sigma^s(h_0)$.
The entries of each conjugate are independent by the field automorphism.
The first $d$ successive conjugates among $h_s$ for $s\in I$ form a basis by the Moore determinant.
Each $W_s$ is symmetric and has columns in the extension-field span of $\mathcal U$ by its definition from the stack.
A left inverse of $\mathcal U$ gives a unique symmetric $\Xi_s$ with $W_s=\mathcal U\Xi_s\mathcal U^\top$.
The ties become $\Xi_s h_{s'}=\Xi_{s'} h_s$ by applying this left inverse.
Any relation $\sum_s\varrho_s h_s=0$ implies $(\sum_s\varrho_s\Xi_s)h_{s'}=0$ for each $s'$ by the ties.
Thus $\sum_s\varrho_s\Xi_s=0$ because the $h_{s'}$ span.
Consequently $h_s\mapsto\Xi_s$ extends to a linear map $\Xi$.
Its trilinear form $\Xi(h;u,u')=u^\top\Xi(h)u'$ is symmetric in its last two inputs.
The ties give symmetry in its first and last inputs on spanning vectors.
Hence it is symmetric in all three inputs.
The form is nonzero because $W_U,W_V$ together contain all coefficients of the nonzero stack.
The matrices $W_s$ obey the Booleanity tests since they are combinations of passing $W_c$ over the extension field.
Those tests give $\Xi(h_s;u_j,u_j-u_0)=0$ for every $j\in[N]$.
By linearity these equations hold with every $h$ in place of $h_s$.
The even exponents of $W_V$ give $W_V=\sigma^{n/2}(W_V)$.
The identity $\sigma^n=\mathrm{id}$ gives $W_U=\sigma^{n/2-1}(\sigma^{n/2+1}(W_U))$.
Since $\mathcal U$ is over $\mathbb F_q$, these equalities give $\Xi_s=\sigma^s(\Xi_{n-s})$ for $s\in\{n/2-1,n/2\}$.

If $u_0=0$, choose a basis $l_1,\dots,l_d$ among the other rows.
Booleanity and symmetry make every basis entry with a repeated index zero.
A nonzero entry then requires $d=3$.
Write $t=\Xi(l_1;l_2,l_3)$, the common entry on permutations of the three distinct indices.
In this basis $\Xi(h_s;l_b,l_c)$ for distinct $b,c$ is $t$ times the coordinate of $h_s$ at the remaining $l_a$.
Comparing these entries in the Frobenius equalities gives $t h_s=\sigma^s(t)h_0$ since $\sigma^s(h_{n-s})=h_0$.
For $t\ne0$ both $h_{n/2-1}$ and $h_{n/2}$ are multiples of $h_0$.
This contradicts their independence in the Moore basis.
Thus $u_0\ne0$.

Complete $l_0=u_0$ to a basis $l_0,\dots,l_{d-1}$ using other rows.
For each $\delta\in\{0,1\}^{d-1}$ let $p_\delta$ be the unique vector over $\mathbb F_q$ with evaluations $(1,\delta)$ on this basis.
Define $w_\delta=\mathcal U p_\delta$.
By symmetry and Booleanity, a basis entry of $\Xi$ depends only on its set of positive indices, since one occurrence of a repeated positive index can be replaced by $0$.
The cubic evaluation tensor of $p_\delta$ on a basis triple is one exactly when its set of positive indices lies in the support of $\delta$.
Inclusion ordering makes this incidence matrix triangular with diagonal one.
Consequently $\Xi(h)=\sum_\delta c_\delta(h^\top p_\delta)p_\delta p_\delta^\top$ for extension-field coefficients $c_\delta$.
The matrix of the $p_\delta p_\delta^\top$ evaluated on basis pairs has the same incidence rows, since every subset of positive indices occurs on a pair for $d-1\le2$.
Hence these squares are linearly independent.
Let $\bar z_\delta=z(w_\delta)$, which is nonzero because $(w_\delta)_0=1$ and there is no kernel vector.
The expansion gives $\Xi_s=\sum_\delta c_\delta\sigma^s(\bar z_\delta)p_\delta p_\delta^\top$.
Comparing square coefficients in the Frobenius equalities gives $c_\delta\sigma^s(\bar z_\delta)=\sigma^s(c_\delta)\bar z_\delta$ for $s\in\{n/2-1,n/2\}$.
Thus $c_\delta/\bar z_\delta$ is fixed by both consecutive powers.
It is fixed by $\sigma$ by composing one power with the inverse of the other.
Write $c_\delta=\chi_\delta\bar z_\delta$ with $\chi_\delta\in\mathbb F_q$.

For each linear test $\varrho$, $\varrho(W_s)=0$ because all $W_c$ pass.
Let $\mathcal Q=\sum_\delta\chi_\delta\varrho(w_\delta w_\delta^\top)p_\delta p_\delta^\top$.
The expansion of $W_s$ then gives $h_0^\top\mathcal Q h_s=0$ for every $s\in I$.
Hence $h_0^\top\mathcal Q=0$ because the $h_s$ span.
The independence of the entries of $h_0$ makes $\mathcal Q=0$, since $\mathcal Q$ is over $\mathbb F_q$.
Independence of the squares gives $\chi_\delta\varrho(w_\delta w_\delta^\top)=0$ for every $\delta$.
Some $\chi_\delta$ is nonzero because $\Xi$ is nonzero.
For this $\delta$ all tests of $w_\delta w_\delta^\top$ pass.
The Booleanity tests give $(w_\delta)_j^2=(w_\delta)_j$ at each coordinate because $(w_\delta)_0=1$.
The constraint tests give the quadratic constraints because each term on this matrix factors into its two evaluations at $w_\delta$.
Each solution of $(w_\delta)_j^2=(w_\delta)_j$ lies in $\{0,1\}$ because $\mathbb F_q$ is a field.
Thus $w_\delta$ is a witness in $\mathcal V$.

edges.demand: Every nonzero v with v_0 = 0 and gp(v^⊤) > θ has an integer x with ‖x‖_∞ ≤ β, x_0 = 0 and x ≡ c·v mod q for some c ≠ 0.
edges.slack: This is the only arrow that leaves the six-node inverse-theorem module.

edges.demand: X^k sums over a coset of order ν to ν·δ^k if ν divides k, and to zero otherwise.
The Moore determinant of elements that are linearly independent over F_q is nonzero.

discharge.argument: The statement directly supplies the bound under (P5) for the stated query range.
Clauses (a), (b), and (c) give the rank bound, existence of a short multiple for a kernel vector of the row space, and the Module-SIS property of its packing.
Clause (a) supplies rank at most three.
The identities give the corresponding divisibility with an allowed remainder. Both directions give passing, and the key-cell divisibility forces its corner to be chi.
The witness clause gives both exact divisions with unit key coefficient, and the general conclusion gives the allowed remainder and respective degree bounds.
The statement supplies exactly the witness conclusion at rank at most three under nonzero usability and absence of a kernel vector.
